title: Space Tourism Awareness
desc: Understand what suborbital and orbital tourism are, the risks, cost, rules and careers, and how to read claims.
task: Produce a two-page fact sheet on space tourism with flight types, risks, costs, environmental impact and careers.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Facts sourced and dated; risks stated; claims checked; peers rate Meets or better.
modules: What counts as space and why it matters
Understand
The edge of space is a convention, not a wall, and the type of flight sets the experience.
A common line is 100 km above sea level, though some authorities use a lower altitude.
Suborbital flights go up and come back without orbiting; orbital flights circle Earth and need far more energy.
Weightlessness on a suborbital flight lasts a few minutes; an orbital stay can last days.
Balloons reach about 30 km, which is high but not space.
A suborbital flight reaches about 100 km, gives three to four minutes of weightlessness and returns in under an hour. An orbital stay costs many times more.
Explain suborbital, orbital and balloon flights to a peer using one drawing.
Peer can say which is which and where the line is.
Flight types and experience
Understand
Each type has a different ride, training need and risk.
Rocket planes and capsules give a quick, strong acceleration; balloons give a slow, quiet ride.
Training: days or weeks of preparation, including emergency drills.
Medical screening checks heart, blood pressure and other conditions.
Comfort limits include seat size and height.
A passenger spends two days in training, including a centrifuge session that shows high acceleration. Another selects a balloon flight because they are not fit for high acceleration.
Compare three flight types in a table.
Table has altitude, time, training and key risks.
Safety, health and informed consent
Evaluate
Spaceflight carries real risk, and the passenger must understand it.
Hazards: acceleration, vibration, radiation, cabin pressure loss and emergency exits.
Operators publish safety records and incident reports.
Passengers sign an informed consent describing risks.
Medical screening can exclude some people.
A passenger reads the written risk statement, asks the operator about abort procedures and decides not to fly until further test flights are complete.
List six risks and a control for each.
Each risk has a control and a source.
Cost, value and who can afford it
Analyse
Costs are far above what most people can pay.
Prices are often hundreds of thousands of dollars or more.
Costs might fall over time, but not soon.
Compare to other life events to give perspective.
Alternatives exist: museum, simulator and educational experiences.
A seat costing 4 crore INR equals many lifetimes of average household income. A simulator ride costs 5,000 INR.
Compare a seat price with local income and an alternative.
Comparison is clear and uses sources.
Environment and sustainability
Analyse
Rocket launches emit gases and soot high in the air.
Black carbon and water vapour affect the upper atmosphere.
Per-passenger emissions can be many times those of a long flight.
Launch frequency matters more than one flight.
Fuel type changes impacts.
One study estimates per-passenger emissions far above a long-haul flight; another gives a lower range. A fact sheet quotes the range and explains the difference.
Check two claims and report the range with sources.
Range stated with sources and date.
Rules, licensing and responsibility
Evaluate
Space tourism is regulated by national authorities.
Launch and flight licences, safety reviews and insurance.
Informed-consent rules differ by country.
Passengers share responsibility for following instructions.
Rules will change as the industry grows.
Operators must obtain a licence for each launch type and must tell passengers about risks in writing.
Summarise the rules in your country or the nearest one with a source.
Source is an authority and is dated.
Careers and ground services
Understand
Most jobs are on the ground.
Engineers, technicians, safety and medical staff, trainers, guides and hospitality.
Data analysts, communicators and finance staff.
Skills transfer from aviation, hospitality, healthcare and engineering.
Local spaceports and launch sites can create jobs.
A hotel catering trainee moves to a spaceport restaurant and a technician from aviation moves into ground support.
Link ten roles to the skills they need.
Roles and skills are realistic.
Write a balanced fact sheet
Create
Combine what you have learned into a short guide.
Use plain language.
State limits and unknowns.
Test with two readers.
Date the sheet and cite each source.
A reader can repeat three facts, name one risk and one cost comparison after reading.
Finish and test the sheet.
Reader can repeat three facts and one risk.

rubric: Each fact cites a dated public source
Each cost and risk figure compared across two sources
Flight licence, consumer and safety rules are listed with dates
Rules checked on the regulator's page and the date recorded
